title: Gideon's fleece (Judges 6–7)
hookLine: the least in his family asks for signs and wins with 300

cards: A young man is threshing wheat in a winepress. That's an odd place for it; you thresh on an open hilltop where the wind can carry the chaff away.
But raiders from Midian have been stripping the land every harvest, so he's hiding, beating out a little grain in a pit.
That's where an angel finds him, sits down under an oak, and greets him with a line that sounds almost like a joke: "The Lord is with thee, O most valiant of men."
The most valiant of men is crouched in a pit, hiding his wheat. His name is Gideon, Gedeon in the Douay-Rheims.

teach.h: THE LEAST IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE.
teach.b: Gideon doesn't believe it. He says, in the Douay: "Behold my family is the meanest in Manasses, and I am the least in my father's house." And he wants proof.

teach.h: DEW ON THE FLEECE, THEN DRY.
teach.b: He lays a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asks God for dew on the fleece only, with the ground dry. In the morning he wrings out a bowl of water. Then, nervously, he asks for the reverse: dry fleece, wet ground.
God does that too, and the text doesn't scold him for asking. Now the army.
Gideon gathers thirty-two thousand men, and God says: too many. The reason is blunt: "lest Israel should glory against me, and say: I was delivered by my own strength." Twenty-two thousand go home.
Ten thousand left, still too many. At the water, God sets apart the three hundred who lap. Some sermons say they were picked for being alert; the text never says that.
They're simply fewer. With trumpets, clay jars and torches, three hundred men throw a vast camp into panic in the night. And Catholics have a second way of seeing the fleece.

teach.h: THE FATHERS SAW MARY IN THE DEW.
teach.b: Early Christian writers, Saint Ambrose among them, saw in the dew falling on the fleece alone a figure of the Incarnation, God's gift coming down quietly on one woman, Mary.

teach.h: I WAS DELIVERED BY MY OWN STRENGTH.
teach.b: Some Catholic readers also hear in the angel's greeting, the Lord is with thee, an echo of Gabriel's. The thread through it all: God picks the least, and trims the army, so nobody can mistake who won.

how: Catholics hear Gideon's call in the Mass readings, and in traditional Marian devotion the dew-soaked fleece is honored as a figure of Mary and the Incarnation, drawn from the Church Fathers and old Advent hymns.

s: the text says the three hundred were chosen for being alert
it never says that. God trims the army so Israel can't say, I was delivered by my own strength.
Gideon asked for a sign twice, and God gave both
first dew on the fleece alone, then dew everywhere but the fleece.
Gideon said his family was the meanest in Manasses
and he called himself the least in his father's house.

games.q: you're Gideon. you have thirty-two thousand men against a huge army, and God says you have too many. what happens?
o: you keep them all and pray harder.
the army is cut to three hundred.
you send for more men from other tribes.
games.why: first the fearful go home, then the water test leaves three hundred. the point, the text says: so no one boasts of their own strength.

practice: Think of one place where you feel short: not enough time, money, people or patience.

Imagine the number going down, the way Gideon's did, and ask what you could still do with what's left: one hour used well, one friend, one honest try. If you pray, hand that small number to God the way Gideon held out his fleece.

wordCard.voice: Gideon's fleece. The sign a frightened judge asked for, twice, and was given. In English, putting out a fleece has come to mean asking God for a sign. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Gideon's name. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, spells it Gedeon.

carryVoice: Your line: fewer is enough. Three hundred men were plenty. That's day three hundred ninety-three.
